top_choice_rationale: P001 (Kiyotaki and Moore, B040) has the cleanest attribution on the slate, since the 1997 originating paper has two authors and every B040 proposal names the same pair. It isolates one general mechanism: collateral-linked borrowing limits feed back on asset prices, so small shocks become large and persistent. After nearly three decades of extension, criticism and use in macro-finance and policy models, it is mature. The citation should claim the mechanism and its influence on how credit cycles are modelled, not a settled magnitude of amplification. Weaknesses I accept: direct empirical validation is indirect, the overlap with the 2022 prize is narrower than it may look but unverified, and excluding Gertler and Gilchrist favours theory over the empirical accelerator strand. The Committee should say so openly. P002 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson, anchored on trade-shock evidence) is a close second. It has credible identification and clean three-author attribution, but it is about a decade younger and its magnitudes and shift-share inference are still debated. P003 (Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn) is a real methodological advance with a mature record, but its credibility depends on functional-form and instrument assumptions, and the credit boundary with Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin is a cut. I rank it above no award, P000, because all three proposals describe substantive, durable contributions.
recusal_note: No tie to Kiyotaki, Moore, Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Pakes, Berry or Levinsohn is apparent from my profile. My co-authors (mainly Kaplan, plus Axelson, Weisbach, Jenkinson, Lerner and others) are not credited on any proposal. I disclose field adjacency: my corporate finance and financial contracting work overlaps with the collateral and financing-constraint channel in P001. I chaired the committee for the 2016 contract-theory prize. I also disclose that I am one of six explicit P001 supporters, including the chair, and I do not treat that as evidence of merit. This is disclosed, not adjudicated.
